profile.reading:
Unlike many entries in this registry, Colovore is a well-documented colocation operator that publishes genuine, checkable technical specifications for its data centers, and the coordinates recorded for this entry correspond to Colovore's flagship Silicon Valley facility, known as SJC01, at 1101 Space Park Drive in Santa Clara, California.

Founded in 2012 by Sean Holzknecht, Peter Harrison, and Ben Coughlin, Colovore built its business around a specific bet: that mainstream colocation, designed around roughly 3 to 5 kW per cabinet, would not keep pace with the power density demanded by high-performance computing. SJC01 opened on January 17, 2014, with more than 9 MW of city-permitted power and cabinets initially supporting up to 20 kW each, dramatically higher than typical colocation of that era, cooled from the outset with a liquid-cooling-capable design rather than retrofitted air cooling. Over the following decade the company pushed density further; its current marketing describes cabinets supporting anywhere from 5 to over 600 kW using direct liquid cooling and rear-door heat exchangers, alongside a target PUE around 1.3 and a water-use effectiveness of zero at its newer builds. Both of Colovore's Santa Clara facilities are described by the company as fully sold out, with new customers directed to a waitlist.

Colovore has since expanded well beyond this single building. It opened an adjacent second Santa Clara facility, SJC02, at 3060 Raymond Street in December 2024, adding roughly 9 MW with cabinet density up to 250 kW, built specifically for AI and machine-learning workloads. The company was acquired by investment firm King Street in 2024, which has funded national expansion into new markets, including Reno, Nevada (RNO01, reported at 16 MW fully committed as of January 2026) and Chicago (ORD01, 6 MW committed as of February 2026), with additional Texas sites announced and under development as of this writing.

What is not independently confirmed is SJC01's exact current square footage or its present-day committed load; Colovore's public materials describe capacity in company-wide and per-cabinet terms rather than a single up-to-date per-building total, and the 9 MW figure most consistently associated with the building refers to its original permitted power at opening in 2014. Subsequent expansions or densification at the site have not been separately quantified in public sources. Even with that gap, SJC01 stands out in this registry as a facility whose owner-operator genuinely publishes verifiable, checkable technical detail rather than declining to disclose it.

reading.body:
SJC01 is Colovore's original Santa Clara facility, opened in January 2014 with 9 MW of city-permitted power and a design centered on high-density liquid cooling. The 9 MW figure is the most consistently published capacity associated with this building, though Colovore does not separately quantify any subsequent densification or expansion at the site in public sources, so current committed load is not independently confirmed. At 20 kW per cabinet, a density Colovore supported at opening, 9 MW corresponds to roughly 450 cabinets; at modern AI densities of 250 kW per cabinet, the same 9 MW would support only 36 cabinets, illustrating how the building's capacity depends entirely on what workload density Colovore commits to at any moment.

The facility qualifies to host high-performance computing and AI workloads through direct liquid cooling and rear-door heat exchanger design, with a reported target power usage effectiveness around 1.3. Colovore describes both its Santa Clara facilities, including SJC01, as fully sold out as of the time the company published that statement, with new customers directed to a waitlist. The company opened a second Santa Clara facility, SJC02, in December 2024 with roughly 9 MW dedicated to AI and machine-learning workloads, and has since expanded into Reno and Chicago with additional Texas sites announced.

California has 103 mapped data center facilities, only 11 of which publish megawatt figures, totaling 365 MW of published capacity statewide. SJC01 ranks 12th by published megawatts among those 11 facilities, placing it outside the state's top ten published sites. The facility's significance lies not in scale but in design: it represents an early and deliberate bet on liquid cooling and power density at a time when mainstream colocation was built around 3 to 5 kW per cabinet, a design philosophy that proved prescient for AI infrastructure demands.
